A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SFTMix study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A.1–A.4 are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Tables 1–2 report original instruction-tuning and healthcare experiments. Section 5 and Appendix A include ablations, human evaluation and multilingual results.

after.justification: The original empirical results are retained, with additional UltraChat hyperparameter sweeps and MT-Bench category results in Appendix A.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the confidence-based split, interpolation of representations and labels, and combined NTP and Mixup objective. Dynamic scheduling is proposed only as future work.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same instruction-following, healthcare and Chinese/French coverage. UltraChat-200K and the MT-Bench categories were already evaluated in v3; the added analyses examine retained coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership remains unchanged, including NTP and IR-DRO in Table 1, the biomedical models in Table 2, and the data-selection comparisons. Figure 5 disaggregates the existing NTP versus SFTMix comparison.

E3.justification: Appendix A.1 extends the reported five-value sweeps for µ and α from Alpaca-52K to UltraChat-200K, adding evaluated parameter configurations for UltraChat. Previously stated training budgets, metrics, judges and evaluation procedures remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Tables 9–10 extend hyperparameter sensitivity analysis to UltraChat. Figure 5 adds analysis of performance across MT-Bench categories. The six main analyses, split-ratio ablation and qualitative example are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report five evaluation rounds for MT-Bench/AlpacaEval-2 and three runs for healthcare accuracy. No seed information, uncertainty intervals or significance-testing procedures are added or changed.

E6.justification: Tables 9–10 add UltraChat sensitivity results, including an overall MT-Bench score of 4.9556 at µ=1, alongside the retained default score of 5.8125. Figure 5 adds category scores, with coding tied. Previously reported results, including the Alpaca sweeps, are unchanged.

T1.justification: The confidence definition, interpolation and loss equations, and gradient/softmax derivation in Sections 3.1–3.4 are unchanged. No formal assumptions, proofs or derivations are added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions and effectiveness claims across models, datasets and applications. The new conclusion sentence proposes future scheduling and pretraining research without claiming an achieved extension.

C2.justification: Appendix A.3 newly identifies coding, math and reasoning as weaknesses of both methods and tentatively attributes them to insufficient relevant Alpaca training data. The conclusion adds dynamic scheduling as a future direction; existing limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Implementation disclosures remain unchanged, including eight H100 GPUs, batch size 32, AdamW, preprocessing, and defaults µ=0.2 and α=0.5. The search grids themselves are retained, and no new code or data access information appears.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion and cited works are unchanged, as is SFTMix's positioning relative to instruction tuning, data selection, training dynamics and prior Mixup research.

P1.justification: Localized edits expand A.1, update the description of appendix results in Section 4.1, rename A.3 to 'MT-Bench Result Analysis', and add an analysis paragraph and future-work sentence. The overall narrative and section order remain intact.

P2.justification: V4 adds the Figure 5 radar plot and expands Tables 9–10 with dataset blocks, moving them from PDF page 14 to 13. Figure 4 and Tables 11–12 are repositioned, spacing changes and printed page numbers disappear. Existing figure artwork is retained.

improvement.justification: Extending the sensitivity sweeps to UltraChat strengthens support for the default settings, while the category analysis makes specific weaknesses visible. These are useful, limited gains over v3. A small new overstatement—claiming improvement in every category despite tied coding scores in Figure 5—reduces precision but does not outweigh those benefits.
